beats.caption: NOR flash holds the firmware every board boots from
beats.text: A small 8-pin NOR chip sits on every server, GPU board, SSD and switch. At power-on the processor reads its boot code and firmware from it. It keeps that code with the power off and rarely gets rewritten.

beats.caption: Cells sit in parallel, each with its own contact
beats.text: Cut open, each cell is a floating-gate transistor like NAND's. The difference is wiring: every NOR cell's drain has its own contact to the bit line, so the cells sit in parallel instead of in a series string.

beats.caption: Random reads: any byte, straight off the bit line
beats.text: Because each cell connects directly, the chip can read any address in tens of nanoseconds. Code can execute straight from it (execute-in-place), which is why it stores boot code rather than bulk data.

beats.caption: Write by hot electrons, erase by tunnelling
beats.text: Programming drives a strong drain current so fast hot electrons jump over the oxide onto the floating gate. Erase pulls them off by tunnelling, a sector at once. Writes are slow, but reads stay fast and reliable.

beats.caption: The trade: reliable and direct, but low density
beats.text: The per-cell contacts take space, so NOR is roughly 10x less dense than NAND and tops out near 2 Gb per chip. That fits firmware, not datasets. Makers: Winbond (2344.TW), Macronix (2337.TW), GigaDevice (603986.SS), Infineon (IFX.DE).
